findings.title: User-storage recovery codes are never consumed, so they can be replayed and the same code is always requested
findings.body: `isValid` for recovery codes only checks that the submitted code is in the stored JSON list and never marks it used. `getCredentials` (line ~237) rebuilds a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full list on every call, so every code always looks unused. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` therefore always asks for the same code number (index 0). Any code stays valid indefinitely, which breaks the one-time semantics of the local provider. The `allCodesUsed()` cleanup in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` can never trigger for federated credentials. The new model also has no id, because `createFromValues` does not carry over `recoveryCodes.getId()`, so `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` would be called with a null id if it were ever reached. The new `getCredential()` path is exercised against a provider whose behavior diverges from the local provider on a core security property, and the test cannot detect that.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly-null MyUser
findings.body: `getMyUser(user)` returns null when the username is not in the `users` map, for example after `removeUser` or for a user from another provider instance. `getCredentials` then calls `myUser.recoveryCodes` immediately and throws an NPE. Every other method in this class (`isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) guards against null. Since `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` is now called from the login path via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, this can turn a missing user into a 500.

findings.title: Recovery codes can be created and validated in user storage but not disabled or removed
findings.body: `supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential`, `isConfiguredFor` and `isValid` now handle recovery codes. `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` and `disableCredentialType` still only handle OTP. An admin therefore cannot see recovery codes as a disableable credential, and `disableCredentialType` logs "Unsupported to disable credential" and does nothing. Once recovery codes are written to the user storage they can never be removed through the admin API, which is inconsistent with the OTP handling next to it.

findings.title: Creating codes in user storage leaves stale local recovery codes valid (and vice versa)
findings.body: When `updateCredential` succeeds, the method returns without touching any existing recovery-codes credential in the local DB. The local `createCredential` path likewise ignores federated codes. If a user already has local recovery codes and the storage later accepts the type, regenerating codes in the storage does not invalidate the old local ones. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential while `isValid` can still accept the old local codes. The user then holds two live recovery-code sets, and regenerating codes does not revoke the previous set.

findings.title: Undocumented SPI contract: plaintext JSON list of codes handed to user storage
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw (unhashed) recovery codes to a JSON array and passes them as the value of a `UserCredentialModel`. The local provider stores only hashes. The javadoc says nothing about this format, that the storage receives plaintext codes, or how the storage should report used/unused codes through `getCredentials` (see the replay problem above). Third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` implementations have to guess the contract, and storing plaintext codes is a security-relevant decision that should be stated. The provider id is also hard-coded as `"keycloak-recovery-authn-codes"` instead of using the factory constant.

findings.title: Recovery-key test covers only one happy-path login
findings.body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and logs in once with code index 0. It does not test a wrong code being rejected, a second login that should ask for the next code index, reuse of an already-used code, or the exhausted-codes path (`allCodesUsed` removal and re-adding the required action). The first two would have exposed that user-storage codes are never consumed. The flow also includes a pointless `delayed-authenticator` with a constant `delay` of 0 and a misspelled alias (`delayed-suthenticator-config`), which looks copy-pasted from another test.
